title: La Sarre Chase: Police Officer Suspended 20 Days
article: Police officer Michaël Julien must serve a 20-day suspension for ethical breaches committed during a chase in the streets of La Sarre in 2017.
The Sûreté du Québec patrol officer had been found guilty on two counts by the Police Ethics Committee last August.

He was reproached for breaching his code of ethics by continuing to take part in a police chase that was deemed dangerous. In addition, the Committee ruled that he had endangered the safety of road users by maintaining excessive speed during the pursuit, which took place right in the downtown core on a Sunday around 6 p.m.

In its sanction decision, the Administrative Tribunal sided with the recommendation made by the Police Ethics Commissioner. Michaël Julien received a 20-day suspension on the first count, and 15 days on the second, with the two penalties to be served concurrently.
The Tribunal found that Officer Julien, who had no prior disciplinary record, was a dedicated police officer with good intentions, but that on that day he committed several acts of misconduct.
"Despite the dangerous nature of the situation, of his own driving, and of the pursued driver's actions on the road, he stayed the course," reads the ruling handed down on May 6.
He acted this way despite repeated requests from his colleague to slow down and end the chase, and despite a safer option available to him, namely to proceed through investigation.
The Tribunal added that the fault was not committed inadvertently or briefly, but recklessly and repeatedly, for much of the chase.
It should be recalled that, following this police chase, Jonathan Belley was shot dead by Sûreté du Québec officers as he advanced toward them with a knife.

The Police Ethics Commissioner had already dismissed a complaint from the victim's mother, who alleged excessive force by Michaël Julien and Vanessa Jean during the intervention. The Commissioner concluded that the officers were justified in opening fire on Jonathan Belley, since their lives were potentially in danger.
The Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP) had also determined that the evidence did not reveal the commission of any criminal offence by the officers.
